subcomponents.title: Entity transitions and persistent grouped scenes

criteria.rationale: Every node primitive renders through Node, a motion.div with layoutId set to the stable entity id. Its transition has a layout entry of LAYOUT_T and EASE, with style left/top/width/height taken from props. Persisting entities therefore get layout projection from their old placement to the new one.

criteria.rationale: The requirement is not met for an entity rendered by the kit's Arrow primitive across two consecutive ungrouped steps. Such an entity must animate from its old state to its new state in place. Instead it vanishes and reappears. How the transition works: hostKey gives each ungrouped step a distinct key, `step:${step.id}`. Stage's AnimatePresence therefore mounts a fresh scene host for the incoming step. The outgoing host fades out with exit opacity 0 over ENTER_T, which is 0.35s. What Arrow does: Arrow carries an entity identity (data-presentation-entity={id}) but no layoutId. So nothing projects the outgoing arrow onto the incoming one. The incoming copy mounts with `initial={{ d, pathLength: 0 }}`. Its `d` already holds the new geometry, so it never animates from the old path. Its pathLength only begins drawing after ENTER_DELAY, which is LAYOUT_T, or 0.6s. Result: the outgoing arrow is gone by about 0.35s, and the incoming one stays undrawn until 0.6s. This is the guidance's second failure pattern: both steps stay mounted, but an entity primitive hides the incoming copy until the outgoing copy has faded out. Appear adds the same hiding (initial opacity 0, delay ENTER_DELAY 0.6s) to any entity wrapped in it inside a freshly mounted ungrouped host. Judges B and C cite exactly this material, and it decides the requirement, so their fail verdict stands. Judge A's reason is accurate as far as it goes. Stage uses default (sync) AnimatePresence with absolutely positioned hosts inside one LayoutGroup. Node supplies a layoutId and a 0.6s layout transition with no initial hiding. But that covers only the Node-based primitives. The guidance judges whichever kit entity primitive renders the persisting entity, and says the mode alone does not establish a pass. Arrow is a kit entity primitive, and the delivered sample uses it for its entities `talk`, `link-1`, `link-2`, `link-3`, `verify-link` and `modify-arc`. Node's layoutId path does not apply to Arrow, so A's reason does not establish that every same-identity entity morphs.

subcomponents.title: Verification tooling robustness

criteria.rationale: The preview is spawned directly as `node vite.js preview`, not through an npm wrapper. `stop()` sends SIGTERM and awaits the child's exit. verify.mjs launches the browser inside its try block, so every exit path reaches `finally { browser?.close(); preview?.stop() }`. inspect-presentation.mjs does not: it calls `await startPreview(root)` and then `await chromium.launch()` before the `try` block. If the browser launch fails, `preview.stop()` is never called. The error goes to `main().catch`, which only sets `exitCode`. votes.rationale: The verifier reserves an ephemeral port, closes it, then starts the preview with `--strictPort`. But readiness comes only from polling `fetch(url/)` over HTTP. The child's exit is checked just once per loop iteration (`child.exitCode !== null`), before each request. It is not raced against the request. Nothing reads the child's own announcement of its address. Another process that grabs the freed port could answer the probe before the child's exit is observed, and `--strictPort` alone is not enough. Neither accepted mechanism is present: (a) readiness taken from the child's announcement, or (b) readiness raced against the child's exit.

votes.rationale: All three clauses hold across the public primitives. (1) Props are explicit typed interfaces, not an untyped bag. NodeProps extends Placement and a data-* template-literal DataProps type, with id, className, style and children typed. ArrowProps, BoxProps, SymbolChipProps and Frame/Emphasis/Label (which take NodeProps) are all typed the same way. No Record<string, unknown> appears. (2) Identity hooks come after caller props. In Node, `{...hooks}` is spread first, then layoutId={id}, data-presentation-node={kind} and data-presentation-entity={id}. In Arrow, `{...hooks}` is spread first, then data-presentation-node="arrow" and data-presentation-entity={id}. A caller-supplied data-presentation-* value is therefore overridden. Frame, Emphasis and Label render `<Node kind=... {...props} />`, so `kind` is set by the Node signature and cannot be overridden by the caller, because NodeProps has no kind field. (3) Kit-only props stay off the DOM. Node destructures kind, id, x, y, w, h. Box and SymbolChip destructure Icon and symbol. Arrow destructures from, to, bend, bidirectional and dashed. Only the data-* rest reaches the DOM element. Appear and SceneLayer take only children.

votes.rationale: The verifier reserves an ephemeral port, closes it, then starts the preview with `--strictPort`. But readiness comes only from polling `fetch(url/)` over HTTP. The child's exit is checked just once per loop iteration (`child.exitCode !== null`), before each request. It is not raced against the request. Nothing reads the child's own announcement of its address. Another process that grabs the freed port could answer the probe before the child's exit is observed, and `--strictPort` alone is not enough. Neither accepted mechanism is present: (a) readiness taken from the child's announcement, or (b) readiness raced against the child's exit.

votes.rationale: All three clauses hold across the public primitives. (1) Props are explicit typed interfaces, not an untyped bag. NodeProps extends Placement and a data-* template-literal DataProps type, with id, className, style and children typed. ArrowProps, BoxProps, SymbolChipProps and Frame/Emphasis/Label (which take NodeProps) are all typed the same way. No Record<string, unknown> appears. (2) Identity hooks come after caller props. In Node, `{...hooks}` is spread first, then layoutId={id}, data-presentation-node={kind} and data-presentation-entity={id}. In Arrow, `{...hooks}` is spread first, then data-presentation-node="arrow" and data-presentation-entity={id}. A caller-supplied data-presentation-* value is therefore overridden. Frame, Emphasis and Label render `<Node kind=... {...props} />`, so `kind` is set by the Node signature and cannot be overridden by the caller, because NodeProps has no kind field. (3) Kit-only props stay off the DOM. Node destructures kind, id, x, y, w, h. Box and SymbolChip destructure Icon and symbol. Arrow destructures from, to, bend, bidirectional and dashed. Only the data-* rest reaches the DOM element. Appear and SceneLayer take only children.

first_results.rationale: The requirement is not met for an entity rendered by the kit's Arrow primitive across two consecutive ungrouped steps. Such an entity must animate from its old state to its new state in place. Instead it vanishes and reappears. How the transition works: hostKey gives each ungrouped step a distinct key, `step:${step.id}`. Stage's AnimatePresence therefore mounts a fresh scene host for the incoming step. The outgoing host fades out with exit opacity 0 over ENTER_T, which is 0.35s. What Arrow does: Arrow carries an entity identity (data-presentation-entity={id}) but no layoutId. So nothing projects the outgoing arrow onto the incoming one. The incoming copy mounts with `initial={{ d, pathLength: 0 }}`. Its `d` already holds the new geometry, so it never animates from the old path. Its pathLength only begins drawing after ENTER_DELAY, which is LAYOUT_T, or 0.6s. Result: the outgoing arrow is gone by about 0.35s, and the incoming one stays undrawn until 0.6s. This is the guidance's second failure pattern: both steps stay mounted, but an entity primitive hides the incoming copy until the outgoing copy has faded out. Appear adds the same hiding (initial opacity 0, delay ENTER_DELAY 0.6s) to any entity wrapped in it inside a freshly mounted ungrouped host. Judges B and C cite exactly this material, and it decides the requirement, so their fail verdict stands. Judge A's reason is accurate as far as it goes. Stage uses default (sync) AnimatePresence with absolutely positioned hosts inside one LayoutGroup. Node supplies a layoutId and a 0.6s layout transition with no initial hiding. But that covers only the Node-based primitives. The guidance judges whichever kit entity primitive renders the persisting entity, and says the mode alone does not establish a pass. Arrow is a kit entity primitive, and the delivered sample uses it for its entities `talk`, `link-1`, `link-2`, `link-3`, `verify-link` and `modify-arc`. Node's layoutId path does not apply to Arrow, so A's reason does not establish that every same-identity entity morphs.

audit_results.rationale: This criterion fails if an entity with the same identity in two consecutive ungrouped steps vanishes and reappears. The guidance names one way this happens: both steps stay mounted, but the entity primitives hide the incoming copy until the outgoing copy has faded out. The quoted kit source shows that happening. For ungrouped steps, hostKey returns `step:${step.id}`, so each step gets a different key. Stage then uses AnimatePresence in its default mode inside a LayoutGroup. The outgoing scene host leaves with exit opacity 0 over ENTER_T, which is 0.35s. The kit's Arrow primitive carries an entity identity (data-presentation-entity={id}) but has no layoutId. Nothing links the outgoing arrow to the incoming one, so nothing can morph it between them. The incoming Arrow mounts with initial `{ d, pathLength: 0 }`, where `d` is already the new geometry. Its pathLength only starts drawing after ENTER_DELAY, which equals LAYOUT_T, or 0.6s. So the outgoing arrow has faded out by about 0.35s, and the incoming arrow stays undrawn until 0.6s. It then draws from nothing rather than moving from its old path to its new one. The persisting arrow vanishes and reappears. Node does have a layoutId with no initial hiding, but that does not cover Arrow. The guidance says the AnimatePresence mode alone does not establish a pass. The criterion asks whether an entity with the same identity morphs, and the delivered sample uses Arrow entities (talk, link-1, link-2, link-3, verify-link, modify-arc). The quoted spans establish that this clause of the requirement is not met.

first_results.rationale: All three clauses are met, so I rule the pass verdict from judges A and B. (1) No primitive uses an untyped bag. NodeProps is a typed interface: it extends Placement and a data-* template-literal DataProps, and it types id, className, style and children. ArrowProps, BoxProps and SymbolChipProps are typed the same way. Label, Frame and Emphasis take NodeProps. Appear and SceneLayer take a typed { children }. (2) Identity hooks come after caller props. Node spreads {...hooks} first and then sets layoutId={id}, data-presentation-node={kind} and data-presentation-entity={id}. Arrow spreads {...hooks} first and then sets data-presentation-node="arrow" and data-presentation-entity={id}. A caller-supplied data-presentation-* value is therefore overridden. (3) Kit-only props stay off the DOM. Node destructures kind, id, x, y, w and h. Box and SymbolChip destructure Icon and symbol. Arrow destructures from, to, bend, bidirectional and dashed. Only the data-* rest reaches the element. Judge C fails the criterion because NodeProps and ArrowProps do not include the full motion.div or motion.svg prop contract. The guidance does not make that a fail condition. It fails only an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown>, and says that typed primitives which apply hooks after caller props and strip kit-only props pass. The hand-typed interfaces are not an untyped bag, so C's observation does not decide the requirement.

first_results.rationale: I rule the pass verdict from judges A and B. Only tests/integration/** and tests/e2e/** drive a browser (vitest.browser.config.ts); the unit tests run under jsdom (vitest.config.ts). The two browser-driving test files, tests/e2e/verify.test.ts and tests/integration/inspect.test.ts, contain no fixed sleep, setTimeout or element-count read used as a wait. They call run(), which resolves only on the child's 'close' event, and then assert on exit codes, output and report contents. The setTimeout calls in verify.test.ts lines 85 and 94 are strings injected into page source to create faults; the test itself does not wait on them. The jsdom-only delay at nodes.test.tsx:86 is outside the browser-test scope, and it is followed by a polling waitFor. Judge C fails the criterion because the verify and inspect scripts sleep (sleep(SETTLE_MS), --settle). Those sleeps belong to the delivered verification tooling, not to the tests, and this criterion judges only the browser tests. In addition, verify.mjs waits for each step with page.waitForFunction on data-step-index (STEP_TIMEOUT_MS) before it records the step. The fixed SETTLE_MS afterwards only gives late errors time to surface, and the guidance lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. INT-002's settle assertion checks timestamps in a report; the test does not sleep. C's reason therefore does not decide the requirement.

The presentation-local folder exports two constants that nothing consumes: CARD_SLOTS in entities.ts and SAMPLE_SLUG in meta.ts. SampleScene.tsx imports ENTITY_IDS, GEOMETRY, INTRO, slotX and EntityId from entities.ts, but not CARD_SLOTS. It places cards with the literal slots 0 through 5, and slotX is `40 + slot * 136`, which never reads CARD_SLOTS. Talk.tsx imports only SAMPLE_TITLE from meta.ts. steps.ts imports only STEP_META. The registry hardcodes the slug string. verify.mjs declares its own `const SAMPLE_SLUG` and imports nothing from the presentation. Neither constant is passed as an id, layoutId or key prop. The review guidance says to score a dead or misleading contract under demo-clear-code-boundaries, and a dead-contract fail must name the declaration and the files searched. The auditor does both. The auditor also agrees that the title contract is consumed: SAMPLE_TITLE goes from Talk to Presentation to Header, where browse mode renders it. That clause is met, but the dead exported constants still defeat the pass.

scene-kit.rationale: The guidance says to judge the kit's ungrouped step transition together with the kit's entity primitives that render the persisting entity. It fails the criterion when an entity with the same identity vanishes and reappears instead of morphing. The kit source shows exactly that for Arrow, which is one of the kit's own entity primitives. For ungrouped steps, hostKey returns a distinct `step:${id}`, so Stage mounts a fresh scene host. The outgoing host fades to opacity 0 over ENTER_T (0.35s). Arrow carries data-presentation-entity={id} but has no layoutId, so the incoming step remounts it and nothing links it to the outgoing copy through layout projection. The remounted path's `d` starts at its new value (initial d = animate d), so it does not move from the old geometry. Its pathLength starts at 0 and only begins drawing after ENTER_DELAY (0.6s). So the outgoing arrow is gone by 0.35s, and the incoming arrow stays undrawn until 0.6s. The arrow disappears and is then redrawn instead of animating in place from its old state to its new one. This is the second failure pattern the guidance names: both steps stay mounted, but the primitive hides the incoming copy until after the outgoing copy has faded. The Node primitive's layoutId morph does not rescue Arrow. The guidance judges whichever kit primitive renders the persisting entity, and the sync mode alone does not establish a pass. The auditor's separate point about Appear wrapping every sample entity depends on sample files that were not supplied. The Arrow defect, shown entirely in kit source, is enough to defeat the pass.

engineering-quality.rationale: The contradiction does not hold. The rubric asks that every wait for preview readiness have a timeout. The readiness wait in startPreview is a loop bounded by a 30-second deadline (`timeoutMs = 30_000`). When the deadline passes, it stops the child process and throws. So the wait the criterion is about does have a timeout. The auditor's case needs a scenario the material never shows: a server that accepts the probe connection and then never answers, so the fetch stays pending past the deadline. The rubric says not to fail a criterion on a hypothetical input unless the review guidance names that scenario, and the guidance does not. It names three failures: a readiness wait with no timeout, previewing while the build is still running, and ready-URL parsing that breaks on ANSI codes or split chunks. A missing per-request abort signal is not one of them. The request is also not truly unbounded. Node's built-in fetch applies its own default connect and headers timeouts, though those limits are longer than the 30-second deadline. The auditor agrees the other two clauses are met: build-then-preview ordering in both verify and inspect, and no parsing of printed URLs. Nothing in the material shows an unmet clause, so the pass stands.
